cards.explanation: The answer is swarms of flies. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to Pharaoh, Egypt's king, "…I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses." (Exodus 8:21) He spells out who and where, right down to the houses. Picture a hot day with the bakery door propped open, then picture that times a whole country.

The answer is the LORD's people. The LORD says, "…the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there." (Exodus 8:22) He calls it special treatment. Flies in the palace, flies in the houses, flies on the ground, and Goshen gets none. I once had to share a drawer with dead batteries, and even they didn't buzz at me.

The answer is so Pharaoh will know the LORD is in the land. The LORD says, "In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land." (Exodus 8:22) The sign is that no swarms are found in Goshen, while swarms ruin the land throughout Egypt (Exodus 8:24). A difference that plain doesn't need a speech.

The answer is False. Moses turns Pharaoh down and says, "It would not be right to do that…" (Exodus 8:26) Staying in Egypt means offering sacrifices right in front of the Egyptians. He asks what happens if they do. It's a polite no, friends, and he explains it.

The answer is three days into the wilderness. Moses says, "We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us." (Exodus 8:27) The last part matters, friends, because he is going where the LORD commands. That's a long walk for a pack of people, so I hope somebody brought snacks. Cookies, obviously.

The answer is far. Pharaoh says, "I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far." (Exodus 8:28) It's a yes with a leash on it. Moses just said the trip is three days out, so that leash is a short one.

The answer is True. Moses tells Pharaoh he'll pray, then adds, "…Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD." (Exodus 8:29) That "again" matters, friends. Pharaoh had already promised once and taken it back (Exodus 8:8, 15). Moses is saying it plainly to his face.
The answer is not one fly. Moses prays, the LORD does as he asked, and the text says "not one fly remained." (Exodus 8:31) That is a clean sweep, friends. My bakery has never once been that clean.

The answer is False. The flies are gone, and Pharaoh doesn't keep his word. The text says, "…Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 8:32) "…this time as well…" tells us it's happened before. It's a pattern.

The answer is False. The LORD says He will make a distinction between Israel's livestock and Egypt's, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die. (Exodus 9:4) The next day it plays out exactly that way: "…not one animal belonging to the Israelites died." (Exodus 9:6) There's no fewer, and there's no few, friends. It's none.

The answer is tomorrow. The LORD sets a time and says, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land." (Exodus 9:5) And the text says the next day He did just that. (Exodus 9:6) One word on the calendar, and the day delivers.

The answer is that Pharaoh still refuses to let the people go. Pharaoh sends officials and finds that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. The text says, "But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 9:7) The report is in, and the answer is still no. Wow.

The answer is fine dust. The LORD says, "It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt…" (Exodus 9:9) Handfuls of soot go up in the air, and fine dust spreads over the land. Imagine flour over a whole country, friends. And you thought my bakery was messy.

The answer is festering boils, and it's a hard one to say out loud. The LORD says "…festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land." (Exodus 9:9) That covers people and animals alike. I think this part of the story hurts.

The answer is that boils broke out on them too. The text says, "The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians." (Exodus 9:11) These are Pharaoh's magicians, and the boils reach them just like everyone else. I think that's a quiet kind of humbling.

The answer is the LORD. The text says, "But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses." (Exodus 9:12) Earlier, the text said Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:32). Now it says the LORD did it. That's a heavy thing, friends, so I'll just point at the verse and let it sit. And the story isn't over.
